prompt:
Find all complex roots (with multiplicities) of the polynomial
$$p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{2008}\big(1004-|1004-n|\big)x^n .$$
answer: $p(x)=x\left(1+x+\dots+x^{1003}\right)^2$: the simple root $0$ and the double roots $e^{\pi i k/502}$, $k=1,2,\dots,1003$.

solutions.title: Recognise a square
solutions.body:
The coefficient of $x^n$ in $p$ is $\min(n,\,2008-n)$ for $1\le n\le2008$ (it equals $n$ for $n\le1004$ and $2008-n$ for $n\ge1004$; in particular the coefficient of $x^{2008}$ is $0$).

Let $s(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{1003}x^j$. The coefficient of $x^m$ ($0\le m\le2006$) in $s(x)^2$ is the number of pairs $(i,j)$ with $0\le i,j\le1003$ and $i+j=m$, which is $\min(m+1,\,2007-m)$. Hence the coefficient of $x^n$ in $x\,s(x)^2$ is $\min(n,2008-n)$ for $1\le n\le 2007$, and comparing coefficients
$$p(x)=x\,s(x)^2=x\left(\frac{x^{1004}-1}{x-1}\right)^2 .$$
The roots of $s$ are the $1004$-th roots of unity other than $1$, i.e. $e^{2\pi ik/1004}=e^{\pi ik/502}$, $k=1,\dots,1003$, each simple (since $x^{1004}-1$ has distinct roots). Therefore $p$ (of degree $2007$) has

- the simple root $x=0$, and
- the double roots $x=e^{\pi i k/502}$ for $k=1,2,\dots,1003$,

which accounts for $1+2\cdot1003=2007$ roots with multiplicity. ∎

answer: Only $f(x)=x$ (iterate $f$: the orbit satisfies a linear recurrence with characteristic roots $1,-2,-3$; positivity kills the oscillating terms).

solutions.title: Linear recurrence along an orbit
solutions.body:
Clearly $f(x)=x$ works: $x+4x+x=6x$.

Conversely, let $f$ be a solution and fix $a>0$. Define $a_0=a$ and $a_{n+1}=f(a_n)$; all $a_n>0$. Applying the equation at $x=a_n$ gives
$$a_{n+3}+4a_{n+2}+a_{n+1}-6a_n=0\qquad(n\ge0).$$
The characteristic polynomial is $y^3+4y^2+y-6=(y-1)(y+2)(y+3)$, with distinct roots $1,-2,-3$, so there are constants $A,B,C$ with
$$a_n=A(-3)^n+B(-2)^n+C\qquad\text{for all }n\ge0 .$$
- If $A\ne0$, then $\frac{a_n}{3^n}=A(-1)^n+B\left(-\frac23\right)^n+\frac{C}{3^n}$, and the last two terms tend to $0$; so for large $n$ of the parity with $A(-1)^n<0$ we get $a_n<0$, impossible.
- If $A=0\ne B$, the same argument with $\frac{a_n}{2^n}=B(-1)^n+\frac C{2^n}$ gives a negative term.

Hence $A=B=0$ and $a_n=C$ for all $n$; as $a_0=a$, $f(a)=a_1=a$. Since $a$ was arbitrary, $f(x)=x$ for all $x>0$.

**Answer: $f(x)=x$.** ∎

prompt:
Find all $c\in\mathbb R$ for which there exists an infinitely differentiable function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that for all $n\in\mathbb N$ and $x\in\mathbb R$ we have
$$f^{(n+1)}(x)>f^{(n)}(x)+c .$$
answer: Exactly $c\le0$ (e.g. $f(x)=e^{2x}$); for $c>0$, using only $n=1,2$ one shows $f'\to+\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$ while $f'<-\frac{3c}2$ there.

solutions.title: Example for $c\le0$, contradiction at $-\infty$ for $c>0$
solutions.body:
**$c\le0$ works.** Take $f(x)=e^{2x}$: $f^{(n+1)}(x)=2^{n+1}e^{2x}>2^ne^{2x}\ge f^{(n)}(x)+c$ (also for $n=0$).

**$c>0$ is impossible.** Suppose $f$ works for some $c>0$, and put $p=f'$, $q=f''$. The cases $n=1$ and $n=2$ give
$$q>p+c\quad\text{and}\quad q'>q+c\qquad\text{on }\mathbb R. \tag{$*$}$$

Let $\varphi(x)=e^{-x}\big(q(x)+c\big)$. Then $\varphi'(x)=e^{-x}\big(q'(x)-q(x)-c\big)>0$, so $\varphi$ is strictly increasing.

*Claim: there is $b$ with $q<-\frac c2$ on $(-\infty,b]$.*
- If $\varphi(b)<0$ for some $b$, then $\varphi<0$ on $(-\infty,b]$, i.e. $q<-c<-\frac c2$ there.
- Otherwise $\varphi\ge0$ everywhere, and for $x\le0$ we have $0\le q(x)+c=e^{x}\varphi(x)\le e^x\varphi(0)$. So $q(x)\to-c$ as $x\to-\infty$, and $q<-\frac c2$ on some $(-\infty,b]$.

Now on $(-\infty,b]$:
- by $(*)$, $p<q-c<-\frac{3c}2$;
- but $p'=q<-\frac c2$, so for $x<b$,
$$p(x)=p(b)-\int_x^b q(t)\,dt>p(b)+\frac c2\,(b-x)\xrightarrow[x\to-\infty]{}+\infty .$$
These contradict each other for very negative $x$. Hence no function exists when $c>0$.

**Answer: all $c\le 0$.** ∎

prompt:
The numbers of the set $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ are colored with $6$ colors. Let
$$S:=\{(x,y,z)\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}^3 : x+y+z\equiv0 \pmod n\text{ and }x,y,z\text{ have the same color}\}$$
and
$$D:=\{(x,y,z)\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}^3 : x+y+z\equiv0 \pmod n\text{ and }x,y,z\text{ have three different colors}\}.$$
Prove that
$$|D|\le 2|S|+\frac{n^2}{2}.$$
(For a set $A$, $|A|$ denotes the number of elements in $A$.)
answer: With $n_u$ the size of colour class $u$, double counting gives $|S|-\frac12|D|=\sum n_u^2-\sum_{u<v}n_un_v=\frac32\sum n_u^2-\frac12n^2\ge-\frac{n^2}4$.

solutions.title: Double counting
solutions.body:
Let $n_1,\dots,n_6$ be the sizes of the colour classes, $\sum n_u=n$. For colours $u,v,w$ let $N_{uvw}$ be the number of triples $(x,y,z)$ with $x+y+z\equiv0\pmod n$ and $x,y,z$ of colours $u,v,w$ respectively. Permuting coordinates shows $N_{uvw}$ is symmetric in $u,v,w$.

**Key fact.** For any $u,v$: $\sum_{w=1}^6N_{uvw}=n_un_v$, since for each of the $n_un_v$ choices of $x$ (colour $u$) and $y$ (colour $v$) there is exactly one $z\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ with $z\equiv-x-y$.

Now $|S|=\sum_uN_{uuu}$ and, by symmetry, $|D|=\sum_{u,v,w\text{ distinct}}N_{uvw}=2\sum_{u<v}\sum_{w\ne u,v}N_{uvw}$. Using the key fact,
$$N_{uuu}=n_u^2-\sum_{v\neq u}N_{uuv},\qquad \sum_{w\ne u,v}N_{uvw}=n_un_v-N_{uvu}-N_{uvv}=n_un_v-N_{uuv}-N_{vvu}\ (u\ne v).$$
Summing, the terms $N_{uuv}$ ($u\ne v$) appear once with each sign:
$$|S|-\tfrac12|D|=\sum_u n_u^2-\sum_{u\ne v}N_{uuv}-\sum_{u<v}n_un_v+\sum_{u\ne v}N_{uuv}=\sum_{u}n_u^2-\sum_{u<v}n_un_v .$$

**Estimate.** Since $\sum_{u<v}n_un_v=\frac12\big(n^2-\sum n_u^2\big)$ and, by Cauchy–Schwarz (QM–AM), $\sum_{u=1}^6n_u^2\ge\frac{n^2}6$,
$$|S|-\tfrac12|D|=\tfrac32\sum_u n_u^2-\tfrac12n^2\ge\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac{n^2}6-\tfrac12n^2=-\tfrac{n^2}4 .$$
Multiplying by $2$: $|D|\le2|S|+\frac{n^2}2$. ∎

solutions.title: Roots of unity filter
solutions.body:
Let $C_u$ be the $u$-th colour class, $f_u(t)=\sum_{x\in C_u}t^x$, and $\varepsilon=e^{2\pi i/n}$. Since $\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon^{js}$ is $1$ if $n\mid s$ and $0$ otherwise,
$$N_{uvw}=\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}f_u(\varepsilon^j)f_v(\varepsilon^j)f_w(\varepsilon^j).$$
Write $F_u=f_u(\varepsilon^j)$ for a fixed $j$. Then $|S|-\frac12|D|=\frac1n\sum_j\Big(\sum_uF_u^3-3\sum_{u<v<w}F_uF_vF_w\Big)$, and by the identity $\sum a_u^3-3\sum_{u<v<w}a_ua_va_w=\big(\sum a_u\big)\big(\sum a_u^2-\sum_{u<v}a_ua_v\big)$ (valid for any number of variables, by expanding $(\sum a_u)^3$ and $(\sum a_u)(\sum_{u<v}a_ua_v)$), this equals
$$\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\Big(\sum_{x=1}^n\varepsilon^{jx}\Big)\Big(\sum_uF_u^2-\sum_{u<v}F_uF_v\Big).$$
The first factor is $n$ for $j=0$ and $0$ otherwise, so only $j=0$ survives, where $F_u=f_u(1)=n_u$:
$$|S|-\tfrac12|D|=\sum_un_u^2-\sum_{u<v}n_un_v .$$
The estimate $\sum n_u^2\ge n^2/6$ then finishes the proof exactly as in the first solution. ∎
